body: All official car coverage in Germany is Generation 4. However, some Generation 2 and 3 trekkers and older spillover coverage also exist.
Germany uses black-and-white bollards with white or light-grey reflectors, which become orange at intersections. They may have road number plates or blue attachments on the side.
The official language of Germany is German, which uses special letters like Ä, Ö, Ü, and ß. It is also spoken in Austria, Switzerland, East Belgium, and South Tyrol.
Many wooden poles in Germany feature a rectangular white sticker.
Germany has a wide variety of poletops, but the most common are horizontal bars with uneven hanging insulators, triangle poletops, and various T-shaped poletops.
Road signs in Germany often have black or dark grey backs, which is rare in Europe. Most signs also feature a sticker with an upside-down red triangle on a black rectangle.
Like Austria, Germany has many regional bus stop designs, but all feature the large yellow and green 'H' symbol.
Mailboxes in Germany are bright yellow and feature the black Deutsche Post logo.
Germany has an excessive number of bollards on most roads, appearing roughly every 50 metres.
German town entry signs are yellow with a metallic frame and black text. They can provide useful information like the town, municipality, and county names.
Germany uses blue rectangular kilometre markers with rounded edges and a white border. In rare cases, they can be white.
German pedestrian signs feature five stripes and a person wearing a belt. This design is also used in Luxembourg.
One-way street signs with the word 'Einbahnstraße' are unique to Germany.
“No Stopping” and “No Waiting” signs in Germany often have white arrows on them to indicate the zone.
Wind turbines are far more common in Germany than in any other European country.
Germany's elevation varies by region: the north is very flat, central Germany is hilly, and the far south has large mountains (the Alps).
German area codes can be used for region-guessing.
German postal codes can be used for region-guessing.
Each German state has its own flag, which can help with region-guessing.
Each German state has its own coat of arms, which can help with region-guessing.
Common place name suffixes can be very useful for region-guessing within Germany.
While most of Germany uses B-Type guardrails, some regions predominantly use A-Type instead.
Different regions of Germany use slightly different cycling sign designs, which can be used for region-guessing.
The design of street sign backs (e.g., folded vs. flat) varies by region and can be used for location clues.
The type of connectors on the back of street signs can also be a clue for region-guessing in Germany.
The German Alps, the most mountainous region in the country, are located in the far south along the Austrian border.
Baltic Pines (Scots Pines), recognizable by their orange-tinged trunks, are concentrated in northeastern Germany.
Trees with their trunks painted white at the bottom are a strong clue for northeastern Germany.
The flat, agricultural plains southeast of Regensburg are recognizable by a slight ridge often visible to the northeast.
Vineyards in Germany are mostly concentrated in the southwest, with a few smaller regions further east.
Hop fields are found in specific regions, most notably just north of Munich.
Traditional red brick houses are a common architectural style concentrated in northwestern Germany.
Thatched roofs and rock walls are common on the North Frisian Islands and mainland Schleswig-Holstein, and also appear in coastal resort towns in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
Houses with black slate walls that resemble fish scales are commonly found in a large area of central Germany.
Large, utilitarian apartment buildings known as 'Commie blocks' are a common sight in all of former East Germany.
Bollards with unusually dark grey reflectors are found in specific regions of Germany.
Some bollards in North Rhine-Westphalia have a green cap at the top, although other colors are also possible.
Green bollard caps with the text 'LVR' and a small coat of arms are unique to southern North Rhine-Westphalia.
Round wooden bollards with a painted top are found in Bavaria.
Irregular bollards that are just the black post without a white bottom half are found on K-roads in a specific region of Lower Saxony.
Simple orange posts are most commonly found in Bavaria, but also appear in other southern and eastern states.
Tiny green markers on trees are a clue for Brandenburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
Bavaria uses white rectangular road markers divided into three sections by black lines.
Simple rectangular road markers with rounded edges are found in Lower Saxony.
Road markers with a metallic border are found in Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.
Triangular marker posts are found in several regions, with variations in color and design. For example, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saxony use rocky-looking posts, while others use white or grey posts.
Basic white plates on bollards are found in several eastern and central states.
Bollards mounted on black disks are a common feature in all of former East Germany.
Rhineland-Palatinate is the only state where the information plates on bollards are orange instead of white.
Similarly, Baden-Württemberg is the only state where the plates on bollards can be grey.
White marker posts with a red cap are found throughout former East Germany, but are most common in Saxony-Anhalt.
Fully yellow marker posts are found in the state of Brandenburg.
Yellow posts with a white plate attached are found in Saxony-Anhalt.
Round, smooth concrete poles are almost exclusively found in former East Germany.
Trident-like pole tops can be found in Bavaria, Saxony-Anhalt, and Baden-Württemberg.
Triangle pole tops common in Western Germany resemble those in Czechoslovakia, with some exceptions.
Poles with a thicker middle horizontal bar are found throughout former East Germany.
Curved horizontal bar pole tops occur rarely in Bavaria.
A rare white and black Generation 4 car is found in Hamburg and Frankfurt, and also around London and Ireland.
Germany is divided regionally between Aldi Süd in the south and Aldi Nord in the north.

German street signs vary by city: Berlin uses white with grey border, Munich blue with decorative border, Stuttgart black without border, and other cities like Düsseldorf, Dortmund, Essen, Dresden, Hanover, Nuremberg, Wuppertal, Mainz, Frankfurt have unique colors, fonts, and frames.
Sorbian, a Slavic language, is spoken near the Polish and Czech border and appears on signs in those regions.

City states in Germany have unique bus stops: Berlin’s segmented style with yellow signposts, Hamburg’s red signposts with hexagonal route numbers, Bremen’s simple red-framed stops, and Bremerhaven’s grey and yellow sections.

City-state rubbish bins are recognizable: Berlin uses bright orange, Hamburg bright red with white speech bubbles, Bremen green and grey with orange bubbles, and Bremerhaven generic green with black logo.
Lampposts in Cologne often have bright yellow numbers on black plastic, though similar styles can occur elsewhere.
Half-timbered houses with arches on the ground floor are very common in a region of Saxony.
Shrub and sand-covered hills, rock walls, brick houses, and thatched roofs are unique to the island of Sylt, though some parts look more generic and flat.
Lowcam coverage in Germany is found around Singen and near Switzerland.
A unique Generation 3 black car is found in a safari park southeast of Bielefeld, where 4x4s painted in zebra patterns are common.
A rare Generation 3 car with an antenna is observed in central Hamburg.
